items.title: LEM-3/ANKLE1 nuclease prevents the formation of abnormal syncytium to safeguard neuronal differentiation
items.summary: by Siyu Deng, Chaogu Zheng In animal development, cells exit the cell cycle after a final round of cell division to differentiate into specialized cell types. However, the impact of failed cytokinesis on the fate specification of postmitotic cells, especially neurons, remains poorly understood. We analyzed the Caenorhabditis elegans mutants lacking the midbody-tethered endonuclease LEM-3/ANKLE1, which resolves chromatin bridges during cytokinesis. Using genetic analysis, fluorescence microscopy, and RNA visualization, we found that unresolved DNA bridges lead to the formation of stable intercellular bridges, creating binucleate syncytia between touch receptor neurons and sister cells, which allows thorough cytoplasmic mixing despite independent nuclear transcription.
items.author: Siyu Deng, Chaogu Zheng

items.title: Resistance mutation supply modulates the benefit of CRISPR immunity against virulent phages in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
items.summary: by Rosanna C. T. Wright, Simon C. Lovell, Anna Richmond, Christian Harrison, Eleri Ashworth, Aras Kadioglu, Joanne L. Fothergill, Ville-Petri Friman, Edze R. Westra, Michael A. Brockhurst Only a fraction of bacterial genomes encode CRISPR-Cas systems, but the selective causes of this variation are unexplained. How naturally virulent bacteriophages (phages) select for CRISPR immunity has rarely been tested experimentally. Here, we show against a panel of genetically and functionally diverse virulent phages that CRISPR immunity was not universally beneficial to Pseudomonas aeruginosa , and its fitness effect varied strongly between phages in predictable ways. In addition to mechanisms known to alter the effectiveness of CRISPR immunity, such as encoding a matching spacer or a protective nuclear shell, we show that the fitness effect of CRISPR immunity negatively associated with the probability of evolving receptor-based resistance to the phage via spontaneous mutation.
items.author: Rosanna C. T. Wright, Simon C. Lovell, Anna Richmond et al.

items.title: CFL1-dependency of discrete cell behaviours driving mouse spinal zippering
items.summary: by Abigail R. Marshall, Andrea Krstevski, Henry Crosswell, Rahul Shah, Eirini Maniou, Nicholas D. E. Greene, Andrew J. Copp, Gabriel L. Galea Epithelial fusion is critical for formation of many embryonic tissues. The developing mammalian spinal cord fuses by zippering, through cell behaviours dependent on F-actin turnover. We propose a caudal-to-rostral sequence of surface ectoderm cell behaviours which drive zippering progression in mice, and test the requirement for the F-actin severing protein CFL1 in this process. Key zipper-advancing behaviours are: (i) constriction of supracellular actomyosin cables; (ii) extension of filopodial/lamellipodial protrusions at periodic intervals; (iii) constriction of leading-edge cell borders bringing together protrusions which establish ‘pioneering’ contacts across the midline; (iv) cell-cell and ( v) cell-ECM adhesion remodelling; (vi) zipper advancement through cell partner exchange.
items.author: Abigail R. Marshall, Andrea Krstevski, Henry Crosswell et al.

items.title: Fungal suppression by bacterial metabolite-activated human intestinal γδT-cells is disrupted in Crohn’s disease
items.summary: by Liya Mathew, Sean L. Carlson, Michael Savage, Claire Pardieu, Megan B. O’Brien, Ellie Crawley, Paul Harrow, Ann-Kristin Kaune, Edward Devlin, Emily L. Priest, Marilena Crescente, Kimberly Martinod, James Boot, SoFong Cam Ngan, Marco Gasparetto, Klaartje Kok, James O. Lindsay, Jonathan P. Richardson, Julian R. Naglik, Andrew J. Stagg, Matthias Eberl, Siu Kwan Sze, Carol A. Munro, Neil E. McCarthy Gut symbionts condition mucosal immunity to resist infection by enteropathogens, but the specific microbes and mechanisms involved differ significantly between host species. In higher primates, bacterial metabolite HMB-PP is sensed by a specialized population of Vγ9Vδ2+T-cells, which we now report can potently suppress growth of endogenous fungi in human intestinal organ cultures.
items.author: Liya Mathew, Sean L. Carlson, Michael Savage et al.

items.title: Emotion knowledge is structured in a grid-like coordinate system in the human ventromedial prefrontal cortex
items.summary: by Yumeng Ma, Philip A. Kragel Human emotional experiences vary widely in everyday life, yet they are systematically organized within a continuous affective space defined by valence and arousal. Although this circumplex organization has shaped decades of research, its neural implementation remains unclear. Here, we asked whether abstract emotion concepts are encoded using grid-like coordinate principles in the human brain. During fMRI, participants tracked trajectories through affective space conveyed through morphs of facial expressions and sequences of phrases. We found that ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) encoded affective space with robust hexadirectional modulation characteristic of grid-like coding. This coordinate representation generalized across stimulus modalities, indicating abstraction beyond perceptual features.
items.author: Yumeng Ma, Philip A. Kragel

items.title: SpatioCAD: Context-aware graph diffusion model for pinpointing spatially variable genes in heterogeneous tissues
items.summary: by Hao Wen, Qunlun Shen, Shuqin Zhang Spatial transcriptomics enables comprehensive characterization of tissue architecture, and the identification of spatially variable genes (SVGs) is a critical step for defining region-specific molecular markers and uncovering spatially regulated mechanisms across diverse biological contexts. However, most existing methods for SVG detection overlook cell density variations, a major confounding factor in complex tissues such as tumors, where heterogeneous cellularity frequently introduces false-positive calls. Here we present SpatioCAD, a computational framework that explicitly decouples genuine spatial expression patterns from confounding effects driven by cellularity. SpatioCAD introduces a graph diffusion model that inherently incorporates cell-density-aware conditions to simulate expression propagation, supporting the identification of SVGs across a broad range of expression levels.
items.author: Hao Wen, Qunlun Shen, Shuqin Zhang

items.title: The promiscuity and degeneracy of ten unique RNA base-pairing rules can determine the success of adaptive RNA evolution
items.summary: by Leander Goldbach, Nora S. Martin, Andreas Wagner The topography of fitness landscapes strongly influences the outcome of Darwinian evolution. This topography in turn is determined by the effects of genotypic changes on phenotypes, such as the structure and function of biomolecules like proteins and RNA. Thus, understanding the evolution of biomolecules requires an understanding of the relationship between genotype and phenotype. Here, we study how this relationship is influenced by the fundamental biochemical rules that determine which RNA bases can form base-pairs in RNA secondary structure. To this end, we computationally study the secondary structure genotype-phenotype maps of RNA molecules using all ten possible different such RNA base-pairing rules.
items.author: Leander Goldbach, Nora S. Martin, Andreas Wagner

items.title: Direction-selective retinal ganglion cells encode motion direction uniformly, despite having discretely distributed cardinal preferences
items.summary: by Carlo Paris, Félix Hubert, Felix Franke, Olivier Marre, Matthew Chalk, Ulisse Ferrari On-Off direction-selective retinal ganglion cells (DS RGCs) exhibit broad tuning curves, responding robustly to motion aligned with or near their preferred direction. These cells comprise four major subtypes, each tuned to motion along one of the four cardinal axes: nasal, superior, temporal, or inferior. However, natural stimuli can move in any direction, and it remains unclear whether intermediate directions are encoded less effectively, or whether this cardinal organization nevertheless supports uniform direction encoding. Here, we combined previous electrophysiological recordings of DS cells presented with a moving light bar stimulus with an information-theoretic measure, the Stimulus Specific Information, to estimate the directional sensitivity of small populations of recorded neurons.
items.author: Carlo Paris, Félix Hubert, Felix Franke et al.

items.title: Traction force microscopy using temporal information
items.summary: by Kazuko Hamaoka, Kasumi Kusakari, Hirokazu Tanimoto Traction force microscopy is a simple, non-invasive method that can quantify cellular contact forces at the cell-substrate interface. It solves an inverse problem of determining the force field from measured substrate deformation. Because this problem is ill-posed with a large condition number, it is necessary to suppress the amplification of measurement noise during inversion. Previous studies have employed algorithms such as regularization or filtering that utilize spatial information to discriminate noise and true signals. Here, we propose an alternative approach that utilizes temporal information of the system. This method employs Kalman filter, a simple data assimilation algorithm in time series analysis, to recover the force field.
items.author: Kazuko Hamaoka, Kasumi Kusakari, Hirokazu Tanimoto

items.title: Adjusting for medication status in genome-wide association studies
items.summary: by Amanda H. W. Chong, Christopher Kintu, Yoonsu Cho, Segun Fatumo, Jason Torres, George Davey Smith, Tom R. Gaunt, Gibran Hemani When conducting genome-wide association studies, addressing medication status that is relevant to the trait of interest can prevent biases that could distort estimates of the true genetic effect. Here, we introduce the genetic empirical medication reduction adjustment (GEMRA) method which uses a heuristic search for an empirical adjustment to be applied to phenotypic values of participants reporting medication use. Through simulations we show that the direct genetic effect estimates in the GEMRA approach exhibited less bias and greater statistical power than common strategies such as including medication as a covariate, restricting the sample to unmedicated users or including all samples without adjustment.
items.author: Amanda H. W. Chong, Christopher Kintu, Yoonsu Cho et al.

items.title: Enhancing cell type deconvolution in spatial transcriptomics through incorporating multiple reference panels
items.summary: by Peiyao Zhao, Justin A. Colacino, Ying Ma, Xiang Zhou Spatial transcriptomics (ST) captures gene expression with spatial context but often at resolutions where each spatial location contains multiple cells. Deconvolution of cell-type proportions is therefore essential, yet existing methods typically rely on a single scRNA-seq reference, limiting accuracy when references are incomplete or mismatched especially in complex tissues. These limitations highlight the need for a framework that can integrate multiple references while leveraging spatial information. We introduce SWIMR (Spatially Weighted Integration for Multi-Reference deconvolution), a statistical framework that integrates multiple scRNA-seq references while accounting for spatial correlations. SWIMR models each spatial location as a weighted combination of references, with both cell-type proportions and reference weights varying across tissue locations.
items.author: Peiyao Zhao, Justin A. Colacino, Ying Ma et al.

items.title: Genetic architecture of the murine serum metabolome reveals carboxyl esterases as master regulators of circulating fatty acid metabolism
items.summary: by Gregory R. Keele, Travis Nemkov, Ariel M. Hay, Matthew Vincent, Callan O’Connor, Daniel Stephenson, Grier P. Page, James C. Zimring, Gary A. Churchill, Angelo D’Alessandro Background The systemic biochemical diversity of circulating metabolites and lipids reflects the integrated effects of genetic variation and environmental exposure. Metabolite quantitative trait locus (mQTL) studies in humans have established gene-metabolite associations, but genetic contributions can be obscured by sex, diet, age, medication use, and environmental exposures. Genetically diverse model systems offer a powerful complementary strategy to isolate genetic contributions to the biochemical diversity of the circulating metabolome. Methodology/Principal findings We applied mass spectrometry profiling to serum samples in 541 mice from the Diversity Outbred (DO) population and identified 1,933 mQTL across 240 metabolites, 561 lipids, 43 oxylipins, and 4,465 MS/MS features.
items.author: Gregory R. Keele, Travis Nemkov, Ariel M. Hay et al.

items.title: A common pathogenic founder variant in Rwandan breast cancer cases
items.summary: by Achille V. C. Manirakiza, Shakuntala Baichoo, Annette Uwineza, Damas Dukundane, Eulade Rugengamanzi, Janviere Mutamuliza, Allison M. O. Niragira, Raissa Muvunyi, Jeffrey Besada, Sarah M. Nielsen, Brianna Bucknor, Diane R. Koeller, Caroline Andrews, Leon Mutesa, Temidayo Fadelu, Timothy R. Rebbeck Germline data from African populations remain sparse, limiting characterization of population-specific BRCA1 /2 pathogenic variants (PV). In a study of 175 Rwandan women with breast cancer, 7 unrelated carriers (4% of cases; 22% of PV carriers) harbored the same BRCA1 frameshift PVs, c.4065_4068del (p.Asn1355Lysfs*10), which is extremely rare in gnomAD yet recurrent in European, Asian, and Middle Eastern cohorts. Whole-exome sequencing and haplotype analysis of all 7 carriers revealed a shared ancestral block of approximately 581 kb surrounding the variant, and extended haplotype homozygosity and network analyses confirmed a common founder origin.
items.author: Achille V. C. Manirakiza, Shakuntala Baichoo, Annette Uwineza et al.

items.title: ATP-independent entropy-driven dsRNA unwinding by DDX3X revealed by coarse-grained simulations and deep learning
items.summary: by Kang Wang, Chun-Lai Ren, Yu-Qiang Ma DEAD-box RNA helicases (DDXs) are traditionally known as ATP-dependent motors that unwind double-stranded RNA (dsRNA). Recent experiments, however, show that some DDXs promote dsRNA unwinding even in the absence of ATP, raising a fundamental question about the physical mechanism underlying ATP-independent strand separation. Here, we develop a minimal, physics-based coarse-grained RNA model and incorporate weak, specific interactions between DDX3X and dsRNA, revealing the inherently stochastic nature of unwinding events. The unwinding process must overcome an energy barrier, but thermal fluctuations and entropy gain provide a driving force for RNA remodeling. We identify that dsRNA separation proceeds through rare yet obligatory strand-displacing intermediates facilitated by DDX3X.
items.author: Kang Wang, Chun-Lai Ren, Yu-Qiang Ma

items.title: Coupled beta and high-frequency oscillations emerge from synchronized bursting in a minimal model of the parkinsonian subthalamic nucleus
items.summary: by Hiba Sheheitli, Luke A. Johnson, Jing Wang, Joshua E. Aman, Jerrold L. Vitek Local field potentials (LFPs) recorded from the subthalamic nucleus (STN) in Parkinson’s disease (PD) exhibit a distinctive multiscale spectral signature: exaggerated beta-band oscillations (13–30 Hz) coupled to high-frequency oscillations (HFOs, 200–400 Hz), with HFO amplitude being phase-locked to the beta cycle. This phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) has been identified as a promising biomarker of the parkinsonian state, yet no biophysical model has explained how it emerges, what determines the HFO frequency, or how HFOs can exist without beta modulation in the medicated STN. Here we show that a heterogeneous population of excitatory Izhikevich neurons with recurrent coupling produces three dynamical regimes: (i) asynchronous tonic firing, (ii) asynchronous bursting, in which neurons burst individually producing broadband HFO power but without coherent population-level PAC, and (iii) synchronous bursting, which gives rise to beta-HFO PAC.
items.author: Hiba Sheheitli, Luke A. Johnson, Jing Wang et al.

items.title: Ten simple rules for teaching practical AI to health data teams
items.summary: by Eric Just, Aik Choon Tan Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly entered the healthcare discourse, often framed through the lens of frontier models, generative systems, and transformative potential. Yet for many healthcare data teams, the practical path from curiosity to capability remains unclear. Concerns about data privacy, regulatory compliance, brittle systems, and misaligned expectations frequently stall progress before meaningful experimentation can begin. This paper presents ten simple rules for teaching practical AI to healthcare data teams, grounded in real-world data, privacy-first experimentation, and system-level thinking. Drawing on hands-on training experiences and existing educational and methodological literature, we argue that AI education in healthcare must prioritize workflows over models, systems over components, and institutional capability over isolated technical success.
items.author: Eric Just, Aik Choon Tan

items.title: Conditional-prevalence correction for liability-scale analyses of covariate-adjusted binary GWAS
items.summary: by Siyi Chen Adjustment for heritable covariates in genome-wide association studies of disease can induce collider bias, creating spurious genetic associations. Following bias correction, interpretation on the liability scale, which represents continuous disease susceptibility, requires an appropriate conversion from log odds. We derive this conversion under a Gaussian liability model for small genetic effects. The direct effect, excluding pathways through the adjusted covariates, and the collider-bias component share a common conversion factor. We characterize how this factor depends on variation in disease risk across covariate values and extend the derivation to case-control sampling. In simulations, the proposed conversion reduced the effect-size inflation associated with scaling based solely on disease prevalence.
items.author: Siyi Chen

items.title: kri-1/KRIT1 promotes innate immune and lipid homeostasis in the C. elegans intestine
items.summary: by Akshay Alaghatta, Samantha Y. Tse-Kang, Daniel P. Bollen, Khursheed A. Wani, Nicholas D. Peterson, Read Pukkila-Worley Animals must differentially allocate essential metabolic resources in response to changing environmental conditions to ensure reproductive success. For example, adult C. elegans coordinate innate immune defenses during infection and also allocate fat stores to the germline, each of which are required for evolutionary fitness. The genetic mechanisms that integrate resource allocation and host defenses in this context, however, are not fully understood. From a forward genetic screen for novel regulators of innate immune gene transcription, we identified kri-1 , the nematode homolog of human Krev interaction trapped protein KRIT1 .
items.author: Akshay Alaghatta, Samantha Y. Tse-Kang, Daniel P. Bollen et al.

items.title: High quality chromosomal genome assemblies of three human Plasmodium species directly from natural infections
items.summary: by Sunil Kumar Dogga, Jesse C. Rop, Alex Makunin, Fiona Teltscher, Damon-Lee Pointon, Ying Sims, Marcela Uliano-Silva, James Torrance, Thomas C. Mathers, Jonathan M. D. Wood, Sekou Sissoko, Antoine Dara, Dinkorma T. Ouologuem, Arthur M. Talman, Abdoulaye A. Djimdé, Mara K. N. Lawniczak Malaria, caused by mosquito-transmitted Plasmodium parasites, remains a major global health challenge. While P. falciparum accounts for most malaria deaths, the lesser-studied P. ovale spp. and P. malariae also contribute to disease burden across many endemic regions, typically causing milder but chronic infections. Here, we generated high quality, chromosome-level reference genomes for P. ovale wallikeri , P.

items.title: Functional dissection of conserved RNAi pathways in antiviral immunity of several hemipteran insects
items.summary: by Yan Zhang, Zhuang-Xin Ye, Qing-Lu Ma, Bi-Yun Wang, Ji-Chong Zhuo, Hai-Jian Huang, Chuan-Xi Zhang, Jian-Ping Chen, Jun-Min Li The small silencing RNA pathways are crucial post-transcriptional gene silencing mechanisms involved in antiviral defense, gene regulation, and transposon suppression. In insects, the three main pathways are the microRNA (miRNA), Piwi-interacting RNA (piRNA), and small interfering RNA (siRNA) pathways. While these pathways are well-studied in model insects like fruit flies and mosquitoes (Order: Diptera), their functions in non-model insects remain largely unexplored. In this study, we conducted a comprehensive functional screening of core RNAi-related genes in a hemipteran insect, the small brown planthopper ( Laodelphax striatellus ).

items.title: SR-A1 cooperates with TLR4-NF-κB signaling to drive macrophage TGF-β1 expression and Treg induction during schistosome infection
items.summary: by Junyao Shen, Ziling Wang, Chuanhong Huang, Weijie Xue, Yu Wu, Tianyu Fan, Yuanyuan Miao, Chenxu Mao, Jiaojiao Yu, Yalin Li, Lei Xu, Jifeng Zhu, Xiaojun Chen, Yang Dai, Zhigang Lei, Sha Zhou, Chuan Su Helminths induce regulatory T cells (Tregs) to establish chronic infections, promoting long-term persistence of both parasites and hosts. TGF-β1 is essential for Treg induction by initiating Foxp3 expression. Helminth infections are typically associated with high TGF-β1 levels, yet the mechanisms by which helminths drive its production are not fully understood. Here, we uncover a mechanism whereby the scavenger receptor class A1 (SR-A1) cooperates with TLR4 signaling to drive TGF-β1 production by macrophages.
items.author: Junyao Shen, Ziling Wang, Chuanhong Huang et al.

items.title: Interpretable embeddings of speech explain and enhance the brain encoding performance of audio models
items.summary: by Riki Shimizu, Richard J. Antonello, Chandan Singh, Nima Mesgarani Speech foundation models (SFMs) are increasingly hailed as powerful computational models of human speech perception. However, since their representations are inherently black-box, it remains unclear what drives their alignment with brain responses. To remedy this, we built linear encoding models from six interpretable feature families: mel-spectrogram, Gabor filter bank features, speech presence, phonetic, syntactic, and semantic features, and contextualized embeddings from three state-of-the-art SFMs (Whisper, HuBERT, WavLM), quantifying electrocorticography (ECoG) response variance shared between feature classes. Variance-partitioning analyses revealed several key insights: First, the SFMs’ alignment with the brain can be mostly accounted for by their ability to learn and encode simple interpretable speech features.
items.author: Riki Shimizu, Richard J. Antonello, Chandan Singh et al.

items.title: Degeneracy in neuronal bifurcation landscapes: Equivalent bifurcation sequences across distinct parameter sets
items.summary: by Gianmarco Cafaro, Christophe Bernard, Meysam Hashemi, Damien Depannemaecker Degeneracy, the capacity of structurally distinct systems to achieve similar functions, is a fundamental property of living organisms, enabling adaptability and resilience. Neurons can maintain stable activity patterns despite substantial variability in ion channel expression, highlighting how different intrinsic configurations can produce equivalent electrophysiological behaviors. Previous studies have shown that neuronal activity emerges from the interaction between intrinsic membrane properties and ionic concentration dynamics. However, how degeneracy is organized within the dynamical landscape of neurons and how different degenerate configurations respond to external perturbations remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate how distinct biophysical parameter sets generate equivalent bifurcation sequences and how their resilience changes under ionic modulation.
items.author: Gianmarco Cafaro, Christophe Bernard, Meysam Hashemi et al.

items.title: Transient feedforward communication between somatosensory and premotor cortex supports goal-directed behavior
items.summary: by Yadollah Ranjbar-Slamloo, Tsukasa Kamigaki Goal-directed behavior requires sensory information to be transformed into motor commands, yet the precise temporal structure of communication between sensory and motor cortices during this process remains poorly understood. By simultaneously recording spiking activity from primary somatosensory cortex (S1) and secondary motor cortex (M2) in mice performing a tactile delayed go/no-go task, we identified a brief, stimulus-triggered communication window that predicted behavioral success. Time-shifted canonical correlation analysis revealed a sharp, feedforward surge in S1 → M2 coupling peaking at a short latency, as expected for a potentially direct transmission pathway. This transient interaction conveyed stimulus-selective information such that the S1 → M2 communication subspace aligned with stimulus-coding axes in both regions.
items.author: Yadollah Ranjbar-Slamloo, Tsukasa Kamigaki

items.title: Full-length genomes evolve in parallel in a long-term evolution experiment with phage φX174
items.summary: by Eva Bons, Hélène Chabas, Hannelore MacDonald, Alejandro Escalera Ledermann, Sira Ösze, Jenny Dunstan, Nicolas Ochsner, Daniel C. Angst, Sebastian Bonhoeffer, Roland R. Regoes The study of evolution in organisms with high mutation rates requires detailed data on the genomic composition of the population. Here we report on an innovative use of high-throughput sequencing technology combined with rapid experimental evolution that allowed us to follow the genetic diversification of four independent bacteriophage populations for 412 generations in extraordinary detail. One of our goals was to assess phylodynamic methods that use genetic information to infer key parameters of the population history.
items.author: Eva Bons, Hélène Chabas, Hannelore MacDonald et al.

items.title: Viral disease outcomes are indistinguishable between experimentally infected bats and rodents
items.summary: by Maxwell J. Farrell, Samantha K. Tucker, Nardus Mollentze, Daniel G. Streicker A common explanation for bats being a conspicuous source of zoonotic viruses is their purported ability to coexist with viruses without suffering overt disease. Widespread acceptance of the idea that bats have unusual antiviral traits has catalyzed the discovery of unique features of bat immune systems which may have translational value as broad-spectrum antivirals, particularly if they evolved as a byproduct of bats’ unique life history rather than through conventional co-evolutionary processes. Surprisingly, whether bats compared to other host groups suffer less disease from co-evolved viruses or from viruses generally has not been formally assessed.
items.author: Maxwell J. Farrell, Samantha K. Tucker, Nardus Mollentze et al.

items.title: Nicotinic receptor in dopamine neurons mediates learned odor choice
items.summary: by Nobuhiro Yamagata, Nobuhiro Takahashi, Rino Ichikawa, Eru Wada, Momo Murakami, Ayako Abe, Mai Kanno, Toshiharu Ichinose, Norihiro Katayama, Hiromu Tanimoto Nicotinic acetylcholine signaling modulates dopaminergic output in mammalian midbrain circuits and can thereby influence decision-making. In Drosophila , dopamine neurons (DANs) in the protocerebral anterior medial (PAM) cluster convey sugar reward signals and promote approach toward a rewarded odor after associative learning. Although nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) have been implicated in regulating PAM DAN excitability and transmitter release, how this modulation supports specific cognitive operations during learning and memory remains unclear. Here, we tested the role of nAChRs in PAM DANs in odor–sugar associative learning and memory.
items.author: Nobuhiro Yamagata, Nobuhiro Takahashi, Rino Ichikawa et al.

items.title: The lipid raft marker flotillin FloA drives relocalization of the plasma membrane H + -ATPase PmaA as a protective response to calcium stress
items.summary: by Moemi Kawashima, Thomas Krüger, Maira Rosin, Sophie Tröger-Görler, Thorsten Heinekamp, Axel A. Brakhage Biological membranes are laterally heterogeneous and contain specialized microdomains called lipid rafts. Lipid rafts serve as organizational platforms that cluster signaling molecules or modulate membrane protein conformation through their unique lipid environment. There are specific lipid raft marker proteins whose functions remain obscure. One of these proteins is flotillin which has been linked to endocytosis. Here, we investigated the regulation and function of FloA, the sole flotillin homolog in the model fungus Aspergillus nidulans . FloA expression is specifically upregulated in response to calcium stress, which is a regulatory pattern also conserved in Aspergillus fumigatus .
items.author: Moemi Kawashima, Thomas Krüger, Maira Rosin et al.

items.title: Type III CI factors from w AlbB induce cytoplasmic incompatibility via a Host Modification mechanism
items.summary: by Xinjun Hou, Feng Guang Goh, Sen Liu, Yao Liu, Xin Ee Yong, Qingsong Lin, Yu Cai The widespread prevalence of the endosymbiotic bacterium Wolbachia among insect species relies on its ability to invade and manipulate host reproduction via several ways, among which cytoplasmic incompatibility (CI) is most studied. Two non-mutually exclusive models, the Host-Modification (HM) and the Toxin-Antidote (TA), have been proposed to explain the molecular basis of CI. Here, we investigate the CI-inducing activity of the Type III CI factors ( cifs ) from w AlbB, a strain currently being deployed to combat mosquito-borne diseases. This set of Cifs displays conserved subcellular localization dynamics in various insect cells.
items.author: Xinjun Hou, Feng Guang Goh, Sen Liu et al.

items.title: Phagocytosis of SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid- and RNA-containing immune complexes drives inflammatory cytokine production and endothelial dysfunction
items.summary: by Johannes S. Gach, Daniel Kim, Khoa Vu, Michaela Marshall, Christopher Cachay, Aminah A. Rangwala, Gius Kerster, Delia Tifrea, Eric Pearlman, Matthew Zahn, Marit J. van Gils, Christopher C. W. Hughes, Donald N. Forthal The aberrant inflammation that characterizes severe COVID-19 is incompletely understood. Given the persistence of SARS-Cov-2 RNA and nucleocapsid protein (N) and the presence of anti-N antibody during the course of severe infection, we investigated the role of RNA-containing immune complexes (ICs) in driving inflammation. We found that ICs consisting of SARS-CoV-2 RNA, N, and anti-N IgG1 are internalized by primary human monocytes and stimulate inflammatory cytokines and chemokines in a manner dependent on Fcγ receptors and partially dependent on Toll-Like Receptor-(TLR)8.
items.author: Johannes S. Gach, Daniel Kim, Khoa Vu et al.

items.title: Taxonova: Deep learning enables fast and confidence-aware microbiome species-level amplicon classification
items.summary: by Kardokh Kakabra, Shriram Patel, Andriy Temko, Marcus J. Claesson Accurate species-level taxonomic classification of microbial amplicon sequences remains challenging due to the difficulty of resolving subtle variations within conserved ribosomal regions. Traditional similarity-based methods struggle with short amplicons and sequences with poor database representation. No existing method performs robustly across the full spectrum of amplicon lengths, limiting applicability across diverse sequencing platforms and variable-region targets. We present Taxonova, a deep learning framework for both short- and long-read ribosomal amplicons.
items.author: Kardokh Kakabra, Shriram Patel, Andriy Temko et al.

items.title: From 16S rDNA-seq count data to microbial interactions: A comprehensive benchmark of co-occurrence network inference methods
items.summary: by Piero Mariotto, Matteo Baldan, Barbara Di Camillo, Giacomo Baruzzo The study of the ecological interactions within microbial communities is crucial for gaining deeper insights into community ensemble and evolution, enabling targeted modification of the community’s functionality. Many inference approaches have been developed to derive ecological associations. Here, we focus on co-occurrence computational methods, in which associations are inferred from metagenomic abundance data by measuring the statistical dependence between species counts across different sampled populations. The limitations in culture-based experiments have hindered the ability to assess these methods’ validity, leading to scarce application in metagenomics studies. To provide a comprehensive assessment of network inference method performance, we benchmark 18 different computational approaches across a broad spectrum of experimental scenarios.
items.author: Piero Mariotto, Matteo Baldan, Barbara Di Camillo et al.

items.title: Cd47 deficiency in mouse brain under excitotoxic stress
items.summary: by Mehrdad Kiamari, Amalia Perna, Matteo Santoro, Abdel El Ariss, Eloise Berson, Jing Zhao, Chandresh R. Gajera, Edward J. Fox, Kathleen S. Montine, Nima Aghaeepour, Thomas J. Montine CD47, a transmembrane protein with well-established immune and neurodevelopmental roles, was recently identified as an abundant presynaptic protein in humans, non-human primates, and mice. To investigate how Cd47 influences neuronal stress and injury, we performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing of hippocampi from wild-type (WT) and Cd47 knockout (KO) mice exposed to kainic acid (KA) at convulsive (KA25; 25 mg/kg) or subconvulsive (KA3; 3 mg/kg) doses. Integrating cell-type annotations with Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) revealed distinct neuronal and glial gene modules whose co-expression structure differed by genotype and by KA exposure.
items.author: Mehrdad Kiamari, Amalia Perna, Matteo Santoro et al.

items.title: Alzheimer’s disease research must connect vascular molecular phenotypes with physiology
items.summary: by Thomas S. Lewis, Jessica Wagner, Jonas J. Neher Molecular profiling studies have mapped vascular alterations in Alzheimer’s disease, but have not proven a role for them in pathology. Longitudinal studies are needed to link molecular and structural changes to vascular mechanics, hemodynamics, and tissue perfusion. Molecular profiling studies have mapped vascular alterations in Alzheimer’s disease, but have not proven a role for them in pathology. This Perspective argues for longitudinal studies to link molecular and structural changes to vascular mechanics, hemodynamics and tissue perfusion.
items.author: Thomas S. Lewis, Jessica Wagner, Jonas J. Neher

items.title: Recombination rate and efficiency of linked selection in small and large stickleback populations
items.summary: by Hongbo Wang, Chaowei Zhang, Kerry Reid, Juha Merilä Population genetic theory predicts that natural selection will be more efficient in large than small populations because genetic drift reduces the efficiency of selection in small populations. Small populations adapting to new environments can also be expected to evolve higher recombination rates to facilitate adaptation as well as to dissociate and purge harmful mutations. We tested these hypotheses (1) by investigating differences in the strength of association between nucleotide diversity ( π ) and recombination rate across the genomes of nine-spined sticklebacks ( Pungitius pungitius ) from four small freshwater (mean N e ≈ 7 096) and four large marine (mean N e = 376 828) populations, as well as (2) by comparing recombination rates between small and large populations using population specific linkage maps.
items.author: Hongbo Wang, Chaowei Zhang, Kerry Reid et al.

items.title: Fast probabilistic whitening transformation for ultra-high dimensional genetic data
items.summary: by Gabriel E. Hoffman, Christian P. Dillard, Kiran Girdhar, Panos Roussos Statistical methods often make assumptions about independence between the samples or features of a dataset, yet correlation structure is ubiquitous in real data. In statistical genetics, correlation between regression summary statistics due to linkage disequilibrium (LD) between nearby variants complicates downstream analysis. Many methods use LD reference panels to account for this correlation. Whitening transformations comprise a family of methods to remove correlation structure, and are used implicitly by many common models. Here we propose a probabilistic model for data whitening, and propose parameter estimates and efficient algorithms to improve statistical and computational performance.
items.author: Gabriel E. Hoffman, Christian P. Dillard, Kiran Girdhar et al.

items.title: Defective viral genomes of porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus type 2: Generation, characterization and interference effects on viral replication
items.summary: by Hao Song, Guoqing Liu, Yongbo Yang, Meng Chen, Haojie Wang, Zeqing Liu, Xinyi Huang, Tongqing An Porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus type 2 (PRRSV-2) is a major swine pathogen that causes substantial economic losses worldwide. Defective viral genomes (DVGs) are important regulators of viral replication, persistence, and evolution in many RNA viruses. However, the characteristics and functions of DVGs generated during PRRSV-2 infection remain unknown. Here, we systematically analyzed publicly available high-throughput sequencing datasets and characterized DVGs generated during both in vitro and in vivo PRRSV-2 infection. We found that PRRSV-2 preferentially generates large deletion DVGs, particularly in porcine alveolar macrophages (PAMs), and that DVG formation is associated with microhomology sequences, RNA secondary structure and AU-rich sequences.
items.author: Hao Song, Guoqing Liu, Yongbo Yang et al.

items.title: MUCOR-ADVANCE: Uniting multidisciplinary science to defeat a deadly fungus
items.summary: by Sebastian Wurster, Adam G. Stewart, Yiyou Gu, Eman G. Youssef, Teny M. John, Priya Uppuluri, Georgios Chamilos, Scott Filler, Vincent Bruno, Ashraf S. Ibrahim, Dimitrios P. Kontoyiannis, on behalf of the MUCOR-ADVANCE consortium
items.author: Sebastian Wurster, Adam G. Stewart, Yiyou Gu et al.

items.title: Individualised electrophysiological neural field models for the assessment of thalamocortical function in disorders of consciousness: A multicentre study
items.summary: by Lín Cóngyǔ, Prejaas K. B. Tewarie, Naji L. N. Alnagger, Iván Mindlin, Glenn J. M. Van der Lande, Laouen Belloli, Steven Laureys, Lionel Naccache, Benjamin Rohaut, Aurore Thibaut, Jitka Annen, Olivia Gosseries, Pablo Núñez, Jacobo D. Sitt Understanding the neural mechanisms underlying disorders of consciousness (DoC) remains a major challenge, particularly in distinguishing limited awareness in minimally conscious state (MCS) and complete unawareness in unresponsive wakefulness syndrome, also coined vegetative state (UWS/VS). In this multicentre study, we fitted a biophysically informed corticothalamic neural field model to high-density EEG data from two large independent datasets, comprising 203 UWS patients, 270 MCS patients and 74 healthy controls.
items.author: Lín Cóngyǔ, Prejaas K. B. Tewarie, Naji L. N. Alnagger et al.

items.title: Controlled human infection with Plasmodium falciparum- infected mosquito bites elicits antibodies against mosquito salivary protein SG1L3
items.summary: by Carolina M. Andrade, Renate C. van Daalen, Amanda Fabra-García, Sanne Grievink, Geert-Jan van Gemert, Karina Teelen, Svenja S. Hester, Rianne Stoter, Marga van de Vegte-Bolmer, Chris Drakeley, Alfred B. Tiono, Robert W. Sauerwein, Teun Bousema, Matthijs M. Jore Human malaria infections begin with the injection of Plasmodium sporozoites via mosquito saliva. Whole sporozoite immunizations have been used as a model to study immune responses to malaria parasites, having culminated in circumsporozoite protein (CSP)-targeting vaccines and monoclonal antibodies (mAbs). However, antibody responses targeting non-CSP antigens on the sporozoite surface remain poorly characterized. Here, we isolated single B cells from a human volunteer immunized by Plasmodium falciparum- infected mosquito bites, who had acquired non-CSP-specific antibodies that recognize sporozoites.
items.author: Carolina M. Andrade, Renate C. van Daalen, Amanda Fabra-García et al.

items.title: The evolutionary advantage of replacers in the Moran process
items.summary: by Michal Pecho, Josef Tkadlec, Martin A. Nowak Evolution occurs in populations of reproducing individuals. In stochastic descriptions of evolutionary dynamics, such as the Moran process, individuals are chosen randomly for birth and for death. If the same type is chosen for both steps, then the reproductive event is wasted, because the composition of the population remains unchanged. Here we introduce a new phenotype, which we call a replacer . Replacers are efficient competitors. When a replacer is chosen for reproduction, the offspring will always replace an individual of another type (if available). We determine the selective advantage of replacers in well-mixed populations and on one-dimensional lattices.
items.author: Michal Pecho, Josef Tkadlec, Martin A. Nowak

items.title: Early vs late fusion of qMIDS with machine learning based classifiers for oral cancer diagnosis from gene expression data
items.summary: by Ferid Ben Ali, Iosif Mporas, Vaishnavi Balaji, Dickson Ibaranyanakaye, Barbara Carey, Muy-Teck Teh, Sola Adeleke Different fusion architectures of the quantitative Malignancy Index Diagnostic System (qMIDS) method with machine learning classifiers for oral cancer diagnosis from gene expression data are investigated. The proposed fusion architectures are tested on geographically and ethnically diverse datasets and the evaluation results showed performance improvements with late fusion, which significantly outperformed early fusion in more matched model configurations than the reverse in every cohort, although at the best-performing configuration the two architectures were statistically indistinguishable in most cohorts. Inter-dataset analysis showed robustness of the proposed architectures when the training/test samples are from different populations.
items.author: Ferid Ben Ali, Iosif Mporas, Vaishnavi Balaji et al.

items.title: CDH1 loss remodels gene expression and lineage identity in human mammary epithelial cells
items.summary: by Maggie Musick, Chinasa A. Ufondu, Carmen E. Rowland, Micaela E. Brown, Joseph L. Sottnik, Madeleine T. Shackleford, Camryn S. Nesiba, Etienne P. Danis, Andrew E. Goodspeed, Richard Zera, Arthur T. Johnson, Kathryn L. Schwertfeger, Andrew C. Nelson, Julie H. Ostrander, Matthew J. Sikora Invasive lobular carcinoma (ILC) is a common subtype of breast cancer, molecularly defined by genetic loss of CDH1, and subsequent loss of cell adhesion protein E-cadherin, in ~95% of ILC. Though CDH1 loss occurs early in ILC oncogenesis, it is unclear how this facilitates transformation. We modeled early CDH1 loss using “normal” human mammary epithelial cells (HMEC), i.e., finite lifespan cells reflecting early hyperplasia, and targeted E-cadherin signaling using antibodies versus causing genetic CDH1 loss using siRNA or CRISPR/Cas9-knockout.
items.author: Maggie Musick, Chinasa A. Ufondu, Carmen E. Rowland et al.

items.title: The peculiar properties of pericentromeric regions of genomes and their influence on sex chromosome evolution
items.summary: by Deborah Charlesworth Results from recent genome sequences support the idea that the lack of recombination across extensive sex-linked regions (SLRs) in some species may be a pre-existing feature, due mainly to the sex-determining locus being located near a centromere. This would cause it to be affected by the “centromere-effect”, which ensures low recombination rates near centromeres. In such cases, it is unnecessary to invoke any active recombination suppression process, or to debate ideas about the types of selection involved. In this review, I outline the properties of genome regions that recombine rarely, including pericentromeric regions of chromosomes, and discuss SLRs that overlap with pericentromeric regions.
items.author: Deborah Charlesworth

items.title: Conserved spike epitopes persist in generalist bat sarbecoviruses
items.summary: by Matthew B. Frieman Bat sarbecoviruses differ in the range of mammalian ACE2 receptors they can use, complicating predictions of spillover risk. Two new studies in PLOS Biology link receptor breadth with antigenic relatedness and reveal conserved spike epitopes targetable by antibodies. Bat sarbecoviruses differ in the range of mammalian ACE2 receptors they can use, complicating predictions of spillover risk. This Primer comments on two new studies in PLOS Biology that link receptor breadth with antigenic relatedness and reveal conserved spike epitopes targetable by antibodies.
items.author: Matthew B. Frieman

items.title: fruitless is essential for male Aedes aegypti mosquito attraction to female flight sounds
items.summary: by YuMin M. Loh, Alberto J. Thornton, WenWei Loh, Tai-Ting Lee, Wan-Tze Chen, Yifeng Y. J. Xu, Jia Xin Yap, Yuichiro Tsuchiya, Daniel F. Eberl, Matthew P. Su, Azusa Kamikouchi Male mosquitoes locate females through strong and innate attraction to female flight sounds, the basis of mating in the world’s deadliest animal. In contrast, females do not show any sound attraction behaviors. Despite being documented for almost a century, the molecular underpinnings of these behavioral dimorphisms remain unknown. Here, we found that by disrupting the male-specific isoform of fruitless (referred to as fruM ) in Aedes aegypti , fruM mutant males show complete abolition of sound attraction behaviors, resulting in failure of mutant males to locate females for mating.
items.author: YuMin M. Loh, Alberto J. Thornton, WenWei Loh et al.

items.title: From CBASS and Thoeris to Panoptes: Phage sponges and the inversion of bacterial immunity
items.summary: by Ruoqi Zheng, Leiliang Zhang
items.author: Ruoqi Zheng, Leiliang Zhang

items.title: MARK3 promotes host antiviral defense by driving GEF-H1–mediated TBK1 activation
items.summary: by Xingmei Qi, Xue Zhu, Wenbiao Peng, Luoxue Hua, Xinru Xie, Chuncan Si, Meimei Lan, Zifan Zhuang, Siyi Ding, Ting Xu, Junjie Li, Yundi Zhang, Yifan Song, Yiping Yang, Yixue Cheng, Tao Guo, Linchao Li, Kezhen Wang Innate immunity constitutes the body’s first line of defense against pathogenic challenge, serving not only as a physical and cellular bulwark that rapidly curbs microbial proliferation but also as the essential rheostat that orchestrates downstream adaptive immune responses. Here, we identified MARK3, a serine/threonine protein kinase of the conserved MARK family, as a crucial regulator of innate antiviral immunity that promotes type I interferon (IFN-I) production in a kinase-dependent manner.
items.author: Xingmei Qi, Xue Zhu, Wenbiao Peng et al.

items.title: Structural basis for inhibition of the lipid flippase MurJ by phage lysis protein Sgl PP7 suggests convergent evolution with other Sgl peptides
items.summary: by Kaito Hosoda, Hidetaka Kohga, Sixian Wu, Hiroyuki Tanaka, Hideki Shigematsu, Ryoji Miyazaki, Min Fey Chek, Tomoya Tsukazaki Some bacteriophages encode lysis proteins that inhibit essential bacterial processes, and elucidating their mechanisms is valuable for developing antibacterial strategies against drug-resistant pathogens. We determined the cryo-EM structure of the complex between the essential Escherichia coli lipid II flippase MurJ and the phage lysis protein Sgl PP7 . Structural, mutational, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulation analyses revealed that Sgl PP7 binds along the intramembrane cleft of MurJ and inserts its C-terminal tail into the internal cavity, stabilizing MurJ in an outward-facing conformation.
items.author: Kaito Hosoda, Hidetaka Kohga, Sixian Wu et al.

items.title: Pollinator abundance shapes sexual selection in an angiosperm
items.summary: by Estelle Barbot, Mathilde Dufaÿ, Tim Janicke, Benoit Lapeyre, Denis Orcel, François Rousset, Jeanne Tonnabel Sexual selection is a central force in evolutionary biology that has been shown to shape phenotypes and population dynamics in animals. While this selective force is increasingly recognized in flowering plants, theory predicts that anisogamy generates sex differences in the fitness benefits of acquiring additional mates—a pattern well supported in animals but with limited tests in plants. Plant studies rely solely on genetic parentage analyses to estimate mate numbers, thereby conflating performance in accessing mates with success in gamete fertilization. Pollinators add an ecological layer, as their behavior and abundance can influence competition for access to mates and their gametes.
items.author: Estelle Barbot, Mathilde Dufaÿ, Tim Janicke et al.

items.title: Auxilin in enteroendocrine cells controls intestinal homeostasis through inter-cell signaling relays
items.summary: by Runqi Wang, Zhengran Li, Jing Wei, Jiajia Wang, Xiyue Liu Tao, Danjie Zhang, Ruiyan Kong, Xuejing Ren, Hang Zhao, Zhouhua Li Adult stem cells are critical for the homeostasis of residential tissue and organism fitness. Residential stem cells must constantly perceive external and internal signals and adjust their proliferation rate accordingly to avoid unlimited proliferation or premature differentiation. However, how differentiated cells affect stem cell proliferation and tissue homeostasis through cell-cell communication still remains poorly understood. Here, we unveil an unprecedented function of Auxilin (Aux) in enteroendocrine cells (EEs) by restricting intestinal stem cell (ISC) proliferation. aux depletion in all EEs leads to intestinal homeostasis disruption.
items.author: Runqi Wang, Zhengran Li, Jing Wei et al.

items.title: Extensive mobilome heterogeneity in a widespread endosymbiont: A candidate dimeric plasmid and highly fragmented prophages in Wolbachia from Culex pipiens
items.summary: by Alice Brunner, Maxime Mahout, Julien Amoros, Massilva Rahmoun, Mateo Jarry, Seth R. Bordenstein, Sarah R. Bordenstein, Blandine Trouche, Julie Reveillaud The obligate, intracellular bacteria Wolbachia have gained increasing interest due to their selfish modifications of host arthropod reproduction, impacts on host evolution, and utility in vector control efforts to reduce arbovirus transmission worldwide. Despite their highly reduced genomes, Wolbachia harbor a rich mobilome that includes phages, insertion sequences and plasmids in mosquito vectors. However, these repeat-rich mobile genetic elements are notoriously difficult to assemble and can generate artificial, chimeric sequences that obscure their true diversity. As a result, conventional genome sequencing and assembly approaches often fail to resolve the complexity, leaving critical gaps of knowledge on how these elements evolve, mobilize, and shape both symbiont and host genomes.
items.author: Alice Brunner, Maxime Mahout, Julien Amoros et al.

items.title: Distinct core minor pilin complexes prime specialized type IV filaments in cyanobacteria
items.summary: by Nils Schuergers, Lars Wittig, Gen Enomoto, Julia Herz, Shamphavi Sivabalasarma, Katharina Ruoff, Friedel Drepper, Sonja-Verena Albers, Pitter F. Huesgen, Annegret Wilde The model cyanobacterium, Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 encodes in addition to the major pilin of the Type IV pilus filament, an extensive, partially uncharacterized repertoire of minor pilins. For those cyanobacterial minor pilins that have been characterized, their roles span a surprisingly diverse range of functions. To elucidate the roles of uncharacterized minor pilins in a systematic way, we applied structural phylogenomics across 90 genomes, classifying cyanobacterial pilins into six conserved families that form two distinct putative core priming complexes.
items.author: Nils Schuergers, Lars Wittig, Gen Enomoto et al.

items.title: Removal of VirD2 from a synthetic T-DNA complex of Agrobacterium by the host DNA repair protein TDP2
items.summary: by Benoît Lacroix, Vitaly Citovsky During plant genetic transformation, Agrobacterium transfers to its host cell a single-stranded segment of DNA (T-DNA), as a covalent complex with the virulence protein VirD2, which is ultimately integrated into the plant genome. The covalently bound VirD2 molecule is an obstacle to the ligation of the T-DNA 5’-end to host genomic DNA; therefore, VirD2 must be cleaved from the VirD2-T-DNA complex (T-complex) before the integration is completed. An interesting idea was raised that TDP2 (tyrosine phosphodiesterase 2), a protein known to resolve protein-DNA adducts, could represent a pathway for VirD2 removal from the T-complex; however, this function has not been proven directly.
items.author: Benoît Lacroix, Vitaly Citovsky

items.title: Hydrophobic remodeling of the SARS-CoV-2 RBD large loop attenuates ACE2 engagement and viral fitness
items.summary: by Aojie Wang, Huimin Guo, Haonan Yang, Haojin Chen, Anna Imojara, Bin Ju, Zheng Zhang, Renhong Yan The SARS-CoV-2 Omicron subvariant JN.4 harbors a unique A475V substitution within the receptor binding domain (RBD) but exhibits limited expansion compared to its parallel descendant JN.1. Here, we investigate how hydrophobic remodeling within RBD large loop (residues 475–490) modulates receptor engagement and spike function. Cryo-electron microscopy reveals that A475V induces local remodeling of the receptor-binding motif (RBM) and alters the RBD–ACE2 interaction geometry. Local refinement revealed that the bulky valine substitution disrupts the local interaction network surrounding residue 475, resulting in a 3.5-fold reduction in ACE2-binding affinity compared with BA.2.86.
items.author: Aojie Wang, Huimin Guo, Haonan Yang et al.

items.title: The Trichomonas vaginalis pseudocyst is a viable cell stage with a distinct transcriptome and an intact membrane
items.summary: by Mari Shiratori, Francisco Callejas-Hernández, Jordan C. Orosco, Steven A. Sullivan, Carlos Carmona Fontaine, Jane M. Carlton Trichomonas vaginalis is the causative agent of trichomoniasis, the most common non-viral sexually transmitted infection (STI). Despite its prevalence, low levels of public knowledge and research funding and the absence of T. vaginalis screening or control programs have led to its categorization as a “neglected” STI. Unlike other STIs in the USA, prevalence increases with age, peaking among individuals in their 40s. Both a motile trophozoite stage and a non-motile pseudocyst state have been described for the parasite, although it was long debated whether the latter is a quiescent stage or a degenerate form on its way to cell death.
items.author: Mari Shiratori, Francisco Callejas-Hernández, Jordan C. Orosco et al.

items.title: Comparative S-acyl-proteomics reveals post-translational modulation of fungal purine metabolism for Verticillium wilt
items.summary: by Chi Li, Wenyang Zhang, Shuaifei Cui, Jian Zhang, Yuzhen Li, Xiaoshi Liu, Yang Li, Zhiying Wang, Wenjie Huang, Gongda Li, Chengwei Yang, Shijuan Yan, Jianbin Lai Verticillium wilt, caused by the fungus Verticillium dahliae , is a devastating plant disease leading to severe global agricultural losses. Although the interaction between V. dahliae and host plants has been extensively investigated, the role of metabolic regulation in fungal development and pathogenicity remains poorly understood. Fatty acids serve as metabolic substrates for S-acylation, a post-translational modification that modulates protein properties and functions, yet this process has not been characterized in V. dahliae .
items.author: Chi Li, Wenyang Zhang, Shuaifei Cui et al.

items.title: Multi-omics analysis of high-grade serous ovarian cancers reveals heterogeneity and distinct immunological patterns based upon clinico-genomic status
items.summary: by Jing Qian, Rania Bassiouni, Yuxin Jin, Seeta Rajpara, Monica Neuman, Varun U. Khetan, Bodour Salhia, David W. Craig, Joseph W. Carlson, Lynda D. Roman, John D. Carpten High-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC) is characterized by remarkable intratumoral heterogeneity and variable tissue architectures, dictating differential therapeutic responses. Although BRCA1/2 mutations correlate with improved responses to DNA-damaging agents, how BRCA genotype shapes the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) remains incompletely understood. Here, we integrated whole exome sequencing, total RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics to profile a cohort of BRCA-mutated (BRCA-MT) and non-BRCA-mutated (BRCA-WT) HGSOC tumors. While bulk transcriptomics highlighted global phenotypic shifts, suggesting a more pro-inflammatory milieu in BRCA-MT tumors, spatially resolved analysis revealed how these differences manifest within specific tissue architectures.
items.author: Jing Qian, Rania Bassiouni, Yuxin Jin et al.
